purpose: Reader-facing consolidation of the 46 governed content modules into substantial book chapters while preserving module IDs for claim, source, SME and runtime traceability. The 21-chapter sequence separates a beginner materials path from its advanced follow-up.

targetWordsPerReaderChapter.rule: Editorial target, not a publication gate. Longer only when governed module text, enrichment, worked cases or diagrams add real instructional value; never pad with unsupported settings or filler.

governanceBoundary: Reader chapters are structural groupings only. They add no technical claims, do not replace or merge the 46 governed module IDs, and cannot promote module publication, SME, accreditation or production status. Claim/source review and independent SME review remain bound to the underlying modules.

readerChapters.title: From Plastic Pellets to a Finished Part
readerChapters.goal: Follow the journey from solid pellets to a finished part. Learn the difference between a machine command, what the machine actually did, and the part result.
learningObjectives: Tell the main stages of one moulding cycle in everyday words.
Explain the difference between a command, a machine measurement and a finished-part result.
checkQuestions: Why can a problem show up at the end even if it started earlier?
Why does one good part not prove the process will keep making good parts?
What is the difference between the value someone asked the machine to reach and a value the machine measured?
What information would help link a part back to the cycle that made it?
readerChapters.applyPrompt: Choose a familiar moulded object. Describe how pellets might become that part, then name one thing supplied to the process, one thing measured during the cycle and one thing checked on the part.
readerChapters.evidenceBoundary: Use these learning prompts to test understanding. They do not add technical claims or authorize machine, mould, material, product or site changes beyond the governed modules and controlling documentation.
readerChapters.readingThread: Follow one part from pellets, through the machine and mould, to removal. Notice what each stage passes to the next.

readerChapters.title: The Machine, the Mould and Safety
readerChapters.goal: Understand the main jobs of the machine and mould, and recognise when workplace safety procedures control what happens next.
learningObjectives: Name the main jobs of the injection unit, clamping unit and mould.
Recognise that a stopped machine is not automatically safe to enter.
checkQuestions: What does the injection unit do with the pellets?
What does the mould contribute besides the part shape?
Why does a stopped screen not prove that equipment is safe to enter?
Where should you find instructions for a specific machine or mould?
readerChapters.applyPrompt: Trace the path from pellets to removed part. At each step, name the machine or mould part involved and whether the work stays within normal guarded operation.
readerChapters.evidenceBoundary: Use these learning prompts to test understanding. They do not add technical claims or authorize machine, mould, material, product or site changes beyond the governed modules and controlling documentation.
readerChapters.readingThread: First map what the machine does. Then map what the mould does. Finish with the safety rules that set the limits for every task.

readerChapters.title: Polymer Foundations: Chains, Amorphous and Semi-Crystalline Structure
readerChapters.goal: Build a strong material-science model from polymer chains to the finished part. Distinguish amorphous from semi-crystalline structure, understand what glass transition, crystallisation and melting mean, and use grade-specific evidence to connect cooling history with properties.
learningObjectives: Explain the difference between a polymer, a plastic formulation, a resin designation and a pellet.
Distinguish thermoplastics from thermosets by their chain and network structure.
Describe repeat units, chain-size distributions, branching and entanglement in plain language.
Explain how branching, copolymer sequence and tacticity can influence chain packing without using a family name as a grade prediction.
Distinguish amorphous structure from semi-crystalline morphology, and explain why “semi-amorphous” is usually not the right beginner category label.
Explain Tg, Tc and Tm as different transitions or events tied to a test method.
Describe lamellae, spherulites, amorphous regions and the limits of a single crystallinity value.
Explain how material grade, flow and cooling history can create local morphology differences in a moulded part.
Interpret DSC and supplier property data without treating a laboratory test as a complete part-performance prediction.
checkQuestions: What is the difference between a polymer chain, a plastic formulation and a pellet?
Why does a polymer sample have a distribution of chain sizes rather than one chain length?
How are branching, entanglement and chemical cross-linking different?
What is the difference between amorphous structure and a semi-crystalline polymer?
Why can a semi-crystalline material also contain a large amorphous fraction?
What do Tg, Tc and Tm describe, and why are they not interchangeable?
What are lamellae and spherulites, and at what scale do they describe structure?
How can cooling rate and flow history change structure across a moulded wall?
What can a DSC scan reveal, and what can it not prove about a finished component?
Why must a crystallinity estimate include sample history, calculation basis and method?
readerChapters.applyPrompt: Choose a polymer grade used in a real or hypothetical part. Draw a chain from exact grade identity and material history through heating, flow and cooling to the measured part response. Label each observation, inference and unknown; then explain which tests would be needed to validate a critical property.
readerChapters.evidenceBoundary: Use these learning prompts to test understanding. They do not add technical claims or authorize machine, mould, material, product or site changes beyond the governed modules and controlling documentation.
readerChapters.scenarioPrompt: A learner calls a grade “semi-amorphous” because it has both ordered and disordered regions. Explain the standard beginner distinction, then use a hypothetical injection-moulded PP part to show how local cooling and flow can create different structures without treating one published experiment as a universal rule.
readerChapters.readingThread: Move from the words used for feedstock to chain architecture, then to amorphous and semi-crystalline morphology. Follow how Tg, crystallisation and melting differ; see how the mould’s thermal and flow history can shape local structure; finish with what DSC and grade data can—and cannot—say about a finished part.

readerChapters.title: Advanced Materials: Fibre Orientation and High-Performance Polymers
readerChapters.goal: Apply the beginner materials map to advanced engineering questions: how local fibre-orientation distributions relate to directional part behaviour, how physical measurements and simulations can be compared, and how a high-demand polymer must be reviewed against the whole material-handling and equipment system.
learningObjectives: Explain fibre orientation as a local distribution that can vary across a part and through its thickness.
Separate global flow-path reasoning, local orientation measurements and part-level performance evidence.
Describe what micro-CT observations and simulation predictions can each contribute, and where their limits remain.
Plan directional measurements around product functions, features and cavity identity.
Prepare an exact-grade review covering supplier documents, equipment interfaces and the material’s thermal path.
checkQuestions: Why is one flow arrow across a whole part only a starting picture of fibre orientation?
What does anisotropy mean when you compare dimensions or properties in different directions?
What does a micro-CT measurement tell you that a simulation prediction does not, and what can neither establish alone?
Why should measurement location, direction and cavity identity be preserved?
Why can a family label such as “high-performance” not supply the conditions for an exact grade?
Which supplier documents, equipment interfaces and thermal-history records belong in a material-change review?
readerChapters.applyPrompt: Choose a hypothetical reinforced or high-temperature material. Create two linked but separate review sheets: one for directional part evidence and one for exact-grade/system compatibility. Include grade identity, relevant supplier and equipment document revisions, part locations and directions, measurement methods and conditions, simulation assumptions if used, unresolved questions, and the physical evidence needed to evaluate the part. Leave unknown values blank; do not fill them with generic settings.
readerChapters.evidenceBoundary: Use these learning prompts to test understanding. They do not add technical claims or authorize machine, mould, material, product or site changes beyond the governed modules and controlling documentation.
readerChapters.readingThread: Start with orientation as a spatial distribution, then compare model predictions with physical observations and plan measurements in product-relevant directions. Next, treat a high-performance material as a system review: read the exact grade documents, map its thermal path and check every relevant equipment interface.
readerChapters.scenarioPrompt: A reinforced grade is proposed for a part with a dimension that changes by direction, and the same project is considering a high-temperature alternative. Separate the two reviews: list orientation evidence for the existing part, then list exact-grade supplier and equipment evidence for the proposed material. Mark hypotheses separately from measured facts.

readerChapters.title: How Melted Plastic Flows—and Why Moisture and Heat Matter
readerChapters.goal: Understand how melted plastic flows and how moisture, temperature and time can change the way it processes and the part it makes.
learningObjectives: Explain viscosity as a material’s resistance to flow and why it changes with conditions.
Recognise why drying and heat exposure depend on the exact grade.
Use more than a surface defect to test a possible material explanation.
checkQuestions: What does viscosity mean in everyday language?
Why can a dryer display look normal while the plastic still needs checking?
How can time spent hot change the material?
What other evidence would help distinguish moisture from heat damage?
readerChapters.applyPrompt: Suppose a part has a silver-looking streak. List two possible explanations and one safe observation or record that could help tell them apart.
readerChapters.evidenceBoundary: Use these learning prompts to test understanding. They do not add technical claims or authorize machine, mould, material, product or site changes beyond the governed modules and controlling documentation.
readerChapters.readingThread: First learn what flow resistance means. Then follow moisture and heat through the material’s journey, and compare evidence before naming a cause.

readerChapters.title: How the Machine Prepares and Delivers Melt
readerChapters.goal: Follow how the machine turns pellets into a measured amount of melt and pushes it into the mould. Learn what machine signals can and cannot tell you.
learningObjectives: Describe how a screw-based injection unit prepares a shot.
Explain shot, cushion and pressure limit in simple terms.
Distinguish a speed request from the motion the machine actually achieved.
checkQuestions: What is a shot in injection moulding?
What job does the non-return valve do?
What does cushion describe, and what does it not prove?
Why might actual filling speed be lower than the requested speed?
readerChapters.applyPrompt: For a hypothetical inconsistent shot, list the machine records you would compare and the part observations you would connect to them. Keep a machine command separate from the measured response.
readerChapters.evidenceBoundary: Use these learning prompts to test understanding. They do not add technical claims or authorize machine, mould, material, product or site changes beyond the governed modules and controlling documentation.
readerChapters.readingThread: Follow the pellets as the screw prepares a shot, then see how screw position, speed and pressure describe delivery into the mould.

readerChapters.title: Transfer, Packing and Clamp Behaviour
readerChapters.goal: Connect filling/packing transition, pressure development and mould-closing requirements.
learningObjectives: Explain V/P transfer as a process transition.
Relate pressure development and projected area to clamp demand without using universal settings.
checkQuestions: Why is a transfer position not universally portable?
Why is machine injection pressure not automatically cavity pressure?
When should flash evidence trigger tooling inspection rather than more clamp?
readerChapters.applyPrompt: Compare two cycles with the same commanded transfer point but different achieved pressure histories and state what else you would measure.
readerChapters.evidenceBoundary: Use these learning prompts to test understanding. They do not add technical claims or authorize machine, mould, material, product or site changes beyond the governed modules and controlling documentation.
readerChapters.readingThread: Connect the control transition to what the mould must contain: read transfer and packing first, then relate pressure development to clamp demand.

readerChapters.title: Feed Systems, Venting and Hot Runners
readerChapters.goal: Treat the complete flow path and gas/thermal management as one mould-system problem.
learningObjectives: Treat runner, gate, vent and hot-runner behaviour as one flow system.
Use location and timing to separate restriction, gas and thermal hypotheses.
checkQuestions: Why can a gate affect both filling and post-fill behaviour?
What defect pattern would strengthen a trapped-gas hypothesis?
Why does a hot-runner setpoint not prove identical material history at every drop?
readerChapters.applyPrompt: Map a multi-cavity flow path and mark where pressure loss, gas evacuation and thermal history could diverge.
readerChapters.evidenceBoundary: Use these learning prompts to test understanding. They do not add technical claims or authorize machine, mould, material, product or site changes beyond the governed modules and controlling documentation.
readerChapters.sequencePrompt: Read this chapter as one connected melt-delivery path: feed system and gate behaviour set pressure/flow conditions, venting governs displaced-gas escape, and hot-runner zones add local thermal/residence history. Keep location and timing attached to every observation so a symptom is not reduced to a generic setting change.
readerChapters.readingThread: Treat runner, gate, vents and hot-runner zones as one connected delivery path rather than separate troubleshooting topics.

readerChapters.title: Cooling, Release and Cycle Stability
readerChapters.goal: Explain heat removal, release forces and their effect on cycle repeatability and part condition.
learningObjectives: Explain cooling as heat transfer rather than only elapsed time.
Separate release-load evidence from deformation created earlier in the cycle.
checkQuestions: Why can two nominally identical cycles start from different mould thermal states?
What measurements strengthen a cooling-imbalance hypothesis?
How can ejection marks distinguish local tooling interaction from general part softness?
readerChapters.applyPrompt: For a warped part that sticks on one core, list the thermal and mechanical observations you would collect before changing the process.
readerChapters.evidenceBoundary: Use these learning prompts to test understanding. They do not add technical claims or authorize machine, mould, material, product or site changes beyond the governed modules and controlling documentation.
readerChapters.readingThread: Read heat removal and part release as one stability problem: the state reached during cooling changes what ejection has to handle.

readerChapters.title: Establishing a Defensible Process Baseline
readerChapters.goal: Show how to create a reproducible, auditable process state before optimisation.
learningObjectives: Define a reproducible process baseline.
Document settings, observed response, context and uncertainty separately.
checkQuestions: Why is a screenshot of settings not a complete baseline?
Which events should invalidate an old baseline?
Why should negative experimental results be preserved?
readerChapters.applyPrompt: Draft a baseline record for one moulding process that another competent technician could reproduce and audit.
readerChapters.evidenceBoundary: Use these learning prompts to test understanding. They do not add technical claims or authorize machine, mould, material, product or site changes beyond the governed modules and controlling documentation.
readerChapters.readingThread: Use the baseline module to define a repeatable state, then use documentation to preserve enough context for another competent person to reproduce and audit it.

readerChapters.title: Scientific Process Development
readerChapters.goal: Teach staged experiments that separate filling, restriction, post-fill response and robustness.
learningObjectives: Use staged experiments to separate filling, restriction, packing and robustness.
Interpret response plateaus and process windows without creating universal recipes.
Sequence development studies so each test answers a defined engineering question.
checkQuestions: What does a fill study try to isolate?
Why is a gate-seal plateau system-specific?
How can a pressure-loss study guide investigation without proving root cause?
readerChapters.applyPrompt: Design a staged development sequence for a new mould, naming the question answered by each study.
readerChapters.evidenceBoundary: Use these learning prompts to test understanding. They do not add technical claims or authorize machine, mould, material, product or site changes beyond the governed modules and controlling documentation.
readerChapters.sequencePrompt: Use the studies as one connected sequence: observe filling first, map where pressure demand accumulates, test whether the feed path still transmits useful post-fill influence, then combine the evidence into a documented operating region and define what would invalidate the conclusion.
readerChapters.readingThread: Treat the four studies as a development chain. Each module asks a different engineering question, and the sequence below shows how those questions connect.

readerChapters.title: A Diagnostic Method for Moulding Problems
readerChapters.goal: Teach hypothesis-driven troubleshooting as a reusable method before defect-specific chapters.
learningObjectives: Use competing hypotheses and predicted evidence to troubleshoot.
Choose discriminating tests and preserve unresolved uncertainty.
checkQuestions: What makes a problem statement neutral rather than cause-biased?
Why can a successful adjustment still leave root cause unproven?
What observation would force you to reject your preferred hypothesis?
readerChapters.applyPrompt: Take one defect and write three competing mechanisms, one prediction for each, and one discriminating test.
readerChapters.evidenceBoundary: Use these learning prompts to test understanding. They do not add technical claims or authorize machine, mould, material, product or site changes beyond the governed modules and controlling documentation.
readerChapters.scenarioPrompt: A defect improves after one controlled change. Build two alternative mechanisms that could also explain the improvement, then name one observation that would distinguish symptom containment from repeatable causal recovery.
readerChapters.readingThread: Read this chapter as the troubleshooting method that the later defect chapters reuse: define the symptom, compare mechanisms, predict evidence and test what separates them.

readerChapters.title: Filling and Boundary Defects
readerChapters.goal: Contrast insufficient effective filling with material escaping intended boundaries.
learningObjectives: Differentiate delivery/restriction short shots from boundary-loss flash mechanisms.
Use cavity and time patterns before changing settings.
checkQuestions: What does one consistently short cavity suggest compared with all cavities short together?
Why is more pressure not automatically the right response to a short shot?
Why can local flash persist even when total clamp capacity appears sufficient?
readerChapters.applyPrompt: Create a two-column evidence table for a short-shot event: observations supporting a common upstream cause versus a cavity-local cause.
readerChapters.evidenceBoundary: Use these learning prompts to test understanding. They do not add technical claims or authorize machine, mould, material, product or site changes beyond the governed modules and controlling documentation.
readerChapters.readingThread: Contrast two opposite boundary problems side by side: insufficient effective filling versus material escaping the intended mould boundary.

readerChapters.title: Shrinkage, Voids and Warpage
readerChapters.goal: Connect volumetric contraction, pressure transmission, anisotropy and differential cooling.
learningObjectives: Connect shrinkage, pressure transmission, cooling, orientation and warpage.
Use time, direction and cavity identity as discriminating evidence.
checkQuestions: Why can longer hold time fail to improve a sink mark?
How can post-ejection dimensional change alter a warpage diagnosis?
What would make you reconsider cooling as the dominant mechanism?
readerChapters.applyPrompt: For a bowed reinforced part, write a mechanism map covering packing, cooling, orientation, geometry and conditioning.
readerChapters.evidenceBoundary: Use these learning prompts to test understanding. They do not add technical claims or authorize machine, mould, material, product or site changes beyond the governed modules and controlling documentation.
readerChapters.readingThread: Link contraction to the final shape by following pressure transmission, cooling, orientation and post-mould dimensional change together.

readerChapters.title: Surface Defects, Gas and Degradation
readerChapters.goal: Separate visually similar symptoms caused by volatiles, trapped gas, contamination and thermal history.
learningObjectives: Separate visually similar gas, volatile, contamination and degradation defects.
Use chronology and process boundaries to localise likely sources.
checkQuestions: Why should silver streaks not automatically be labelled moisture?
What timing pattern distinguishes a residence-linked burn from a fixed gas trap?
How can cavity distribution help localise black-speck sources?
readerChapters.applyPrompt: Build a source map for a dark-speck complaint and rank likely locations for an all-cavity versus one-cavity pattern.
readerChapters.evidenceBoundary: Use these learning prompts to test understanding. They do not add technical claims or authorize machine, mould, material, product or site changes beyond the governed modules and controlling documentation.
readerChapters.readingThread: Use appearance only as the starting observation. The three modules then separate volatile, gas, contamination and degradation mechanisms by location and timing.

readerChapters.title: Weld Lines and Flow-Front Interaction
readerChapters.goal: Give weld-line formation, evidence and design/process interactions enough depth to stand alone.
learningObjectives: Explain weld-line formation as a flow-front interaction.
Separate appearance, mechanical consequence and root-cause evidence.
checkQuestions: Why can a visible weld line be acceptable in one product but critical in another?
How do geometry and gate location constrain weld-line position?
Why is increasing melt temperature not a complete diagnosis?
readerChapters.applyPrompt: For a weld line downstream of a hole, identify geometry-fixed evidence, process-sensitive evidence and product-performance evidence.
readerChapters.evidenceBoundary: Use these learning prompts to test understanding. They do not add technical claims or authorize machine, mould, material, product or site changes beyond the governed modules and controlling documentation.
readerChapters.readingThread: Keep formation, location and product performance separate as you read; the visible interface is only one part of the engineering question.

readerChapters.title: Cavity Pressure and Process Monitoring
readerChapters.goal: Explain measurement location, signal meaning, baselines, alarms and limits of inference.
learningObjectives: Interpret cavity-pressure traces in sensor/location context.
Design monitoring rules that trigger investigation without pretending to prove root cause.
checkQuestions: Which parts of a cavity-pressure trace can carry information beyond peak pressure?
Why must sensor position remain part of the interpretation?
What is the difference between a process alarm and a product disposition decision?
readerChapters.applyPrompt: Choose one monitored signal and define its origin, units, baseline, alarm meaning and required follow-up.
readerChapters.evidenceBoundary: Use these learning prompts to test understanding. They do not add technical claims or authorize machine, mould, material, product or site changes beyond the governed modules and controlling documentation.
readerChapters.readingThread: Start with what a cavity-pressure signal represents, then move to how repeated signals can support monitoring without becoming automatic proof of cause.

readerChapters.title: DOE, Measurement and Capability
readerChapters.goal: Connect experimental design, measurement credibility, stability and capability rather than teaching them as isolated statistical topics.
learningObjectives: Interpret DOE effects and interactions with engineering context.
Evaluate capability only for stable, defined populations with credible measurement.
checkQuestions: Why can a main effect reverse across another factor level?
What is the purpose of a confirmation run?
Why can pooled multi-cavity capability answer the wrong question?
What evidence would make a statistically significant result practically unhelpful for the moulding decision?
readerChapters.applyPrompt: Sketch a two-factor experiment and state the nuisance variables, confirmation step and population definition needed before a capability claim.
readerChapters.evidenceBoundary: Use these learning prompts to test understanding. They do not add technical claims or authorize machine, mould, material, product or site changes beyond the governed modules and controlling documentation.
readerChapters.readingThread: Use DOE to structure comparisons, measurement to judge the observations, and capability to describe performance relative to requirements.

readerChapters.title: Dimensional Stability and Measurement Conditions
readerChapters.goal: Explain why a dimension depends on when, where and how it is measured, and how controlled comparisons help separate competing causes.
learningObjectives: Include conditioning, timing, environment and method in a dimensional result.
Use cavity, time and measurement-direction patterns to organise competing explanations.
checkQuestions: Why must measurement timing and conditioning be part of a dimensional result?
How could a time trend differ from a cavity-specific pattern?
Why does a measurement help test a possible cause without automatically proving it?
readerChapters.applyPrompt: Plan a dimensional study that separates conditioning time, cavity identity and measurement direction.
readerChapters.evidenceBoundary: Use these learning prompts to test understanding. They do not add technical claims or authorize machine, mould, material, product or site changes beyond the governed modules and controlling documentation.
readerChapters.readingThread: Define the measurement conditions first. Then use consistent measurements over time and across cavities to compare possible material, mould and process contributions.

readerChapters.title: Thin-Wall and Multi-Cavity Processing
readerChapters.goal: Study advanced moulding situations where machine capability, flow path and cavity-specific evidence become especially important.
learningObjectives: Recognise why thin-wall capability depends on more than one machine rating.
Preserve cavity identity when evaluating balance and part results.
checkQuestions: Why can thin-wall capability not be judged from pressure rating alone?
How can pooling results from several cavities hide a repeated imbalance?
What evidence would help distinguish a cavity-specific issue from a whole-process change?
readerChapters.applyPrompt: For a hypothetical four-cavity thin-wall part, list the machine, mould, flow-path and cavity-specific evidence you would preserve before drawing a conclusion.
readerChapters.evidenceBoundary: Use these learning prompts to test understanding. They do not add technical claims or authorize machine, mould, material, product or site changes beyond the governed modules and controlling documentation.
readerChapters.sequencePrompt: Carry the evidence method into demanding geometries: keep machine capability, flow path and individual cavity response connected to the part result.
readerChapters.scenarioPrompt: A four-cavity mould shows a dimensional difference in one cavity while the pooled average still looks acceptable. List how you would keep cavity identity, machine measurements, mould condition and part measurements linked while investigating. Do not infer a cause from the average alone.
readerChapters.readingThread: Use thin-wall and multi-cavity examples to see why equipment limits, flow path and cavity identity must stay visible in the evidence.

readerChapters.title: Complex Diagnostics and Engineering Judgment
readerChapters.goal: Finish with competing hypotheses, uncertainty, evidence ledgers and escalation rather than false certainty.
learningObjectives: Rank competing hypotheses by evidence, consequence and testability.
Separate containment, corrective action and root-cause proof.
Use contradictions and stopping rules to recognise when confidence is insufficient and escalation is appropriate.
checkQuestions: Why should contradictory evidence be highlighted rather than explained away?
When can a successful containment action still leave root cause unresolved?
How should safety consequence affect hypothesis priority?
What evidence would justify stopping an investigation rather than continuing to tune the process?
readerChapters.applyPrompt: Write an evidence ledger for a complex defect with at least three hypotheses, predicted observations, contradictions and a next test.
readerChapters.evidenceBoundary: Use these learning prompts to test understanding. They do not add technical claims or authorize machine, mould, material, product or site changes beyond the governed modules and controlling documentation.
readerChapters.readingThread: Read this capstone as a decision method rather than a defect list: the goal is to update confidence as evidence, contradictions and consequence change.

reviewQuestions: Does each reader chapter have one coherent learner decision or mental model?
Can every technical claim still be traced to a governed module and evidence record?
Does consolidation reduce repetition without hiding important applicability boundaries?
Are worked cases and diagrams placed where they teach interpretation rather than decorate the text?
Can a beginner read chapters 1–10 sequentially and an experienced technician enter at chapters 11–20 without losing critical safety context?
pedagogyPolicy: Reader-level objectives, checks, application prompts, reading threads, key-term labels and optional reasoning scenarios are derived learning scaffolds only. They add no technical claims, do not alter governed module evidence status and cannot create production authority. Sequence prompts are reader-orientation scaffolds derived from existing governed module order; they add no independent technical authority. Key terms identify vocabulary to notice and do not act as standalone definitions.
depthBandMeaning: Depth labels describe how technical the ideas are; they are not a test of who can read a chapter and they are not a ladder you have to climb in order. The first five chapters start with plain-language explanations and build toward more specialist detail.
firstReadPolicy: The guided reading starts with the main explanation. Notes about where ideas apply, source details and worked examples are available through progressive disclosure: open them when you want more detail. Key terms are navigation labels; the chapter text explains their meanings.
